Aniruddha Dobre 4w Report this post 𝗠𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗳𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗵𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝘄𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗮 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘆𝘀𝘁 𝗷𝗼𝗯. 𝗔𝗹𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗻𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘄𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗮 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘆𝘀𝘁 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘁. Last week, our team interacted with at least 20 candidates who were either working as data analysts or aspiring to become one, mostly at the fresher level. Here's what stood out: most of them came across as job seekers. Very few spoke like professionals who want to grow into authority in the role. The questions sounded like: → "Which company is hiring?" → "How many tools should I learn?" → "How fast can I get placed?" Rarely: → "What does this role look like in 5 years?" → "What do I need to build to be taken seriously?" That gap matters, because a job gets you in the door, but a roadmap decides where you go next. 𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗲'𝘀 𝗮 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘆𝘀𝘁 𝗿𝗼𝗮𝗱𝗺𝗮𝗽: 𝗬𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘀 𝟭-𝟮: 𝗕𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁 Master SQL, Python or R, and a BI tool. Learn A/B testing and funnel analysis. Own an analysis end to end and learn to tell the story behind the numbers. 𝗬𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘀 𝟯-𝟰: 𝗦𝗽𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗲 Pick a direction: analytics leadership, data science, analytics engineering, or business/domain strategy. Choose based on what energizes you most. 𝗬𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘀 𝟱+: 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝘀𝗲𝗻𝗶𝗼𝗿 𝘀𝗰𝗼𝗽𝗲 Lead a team as a manager, or go deep as a Senior/Staff Analyst, Data Scientist, or Analytics Engineer. The skills that compound on every path: ✔ Communication ✔ Business acumen ✔ Data quality instincts ✔ AI-assisted workflows The analysts who grow fastest ask "Where am I headed?" before "Where do I apply?" At 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗝𝗼𝗯 𝗙𝗶𝘁 𝗖𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗿 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺, we run this kind of exercise with every job seeker we work with, so they leave with clarity on where they are, where they can go, and what to build next. If you're early in your data journey, ask yourself: 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗮 𝗷𝗼𝗯, 𝗼𝗿 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗿? Alistair Rodrigues 1w Report this post "Aspiring Data Analyst | Seeking Opportunities" You've probably seen this headline on a lot of fresher profiles. What does a recruiter actually learn from it? Your headline sits next to your name almost everywhere on LinkedIn: search results, comments, connection requests. It's often the only line someone reads before deciding whether to open your profile. "Aspiring" tells them you're not there yet. "Seeking opportunities" tells them nothing about what you can do. Try this structure instead: Role you want | 2–3 tools you actually use | one thing you built For example: Data Analyst | SQL, Power BI, Python | Built a sales dashboard used by a 12-person team One rule: if you can't be interviewed on it, don't put it in the headline. Change it tonight, before Monday's applications go out. It takes two minutes, and every comment you leave this week will carry it.
